newsitem.title: UK: European share losses trimmed, dollar steady.
newsitem.headline: European share losses trimmed, dollar steady.

text.p: European bourses trimmed their losses by mid-afternoon on Friday after Wall Street attempted to stem its decline following a near 100-point drop on Thursday.

They then slipped back again after the Dow Jones industrial average of key U.S. stocks, which had fallen 170 points or 2.5 percent in the past two sessions, headed lower after flirting with narrow gains.

But the Dow, having shed just over 50 points at its lowest, was soon showing a deficit of less than 10 points as the world's biggest stock market sought a level and European bourses watched its every move.

"There's a lot of nervousness and a lot of changing direction out there," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co in New York. "But so far it's not as ugly as things appeared before the open."
Wary currency traders were more focused on the European Union summit in Dublin, awaiting details of a budgetary stability pact to underpin plans for a single euro currency.
EU leaders broke for lunch without agreement on a pact to enforce budget discipline on countries that join a single European currency in 1999, diplomats said.
"It is a pretty tough fight and that's an understatement," Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky told reporters.

The dollar, meanwhile, benefited from heavy U.S. buying and dealers said it also gained against the yen amid market talk that a private Washington-based consultancy had reported that Japan would tolerate a rise in the U.S. currency to 120 yen.
From the opening on Friday, investors in Europe, fretting that Wall Street might be suffering something worse than a passing cold, had taken more profits after a successful year for shares.

Some market watchers have raised the spectre of a major correction after Wall Street gained almost a third in value this year. But London dealers said many institutional investors were still reluctant to sell heavily.

"Institutions aren't ready to aggressively sell," the head of trading at a major investment bank said. "People are still hoping the FTSE won't fall as much as the Dow since it (FTSE) has underperformed other markets this year."
London's FTSE 100 index has risen some nine percent in 1996.
A week ago markets plunged worldwide after remarks by U.S. central bank chief Alan Greenspan on the "irrational exuberance" of the U.S. stock market.
But one London dealer commented: "Even if the Dow falls another 300 points, we're still looking at an annual gain of 20 percent, which is a good performance by anyone's standards."
German and French shares tracked lower along with London. Some Frankfurt dealers had feared worse to come. "After all, it's Friday the 13th," said one.

The Bank of Spain, cheered by sluggish inflation, sanctioned its seventh interest rate cut of the year and dealers and analysts said the cut could reduce pressure for the peseta to strengthen. The mark was quoted around 84.22 pesetas, compared with Thursday's late 84.23.
CURRENCIES AT 1515 GMT
The dollar was quoted around 113.60 yen and 1.5425 marks against 113.33 and 1.5427 in late European business on Thursday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1515 GMT
The FTSE 100 index of top British shares was 38.8 points lower at 3,951.9.
In Paris, the CAC-40 index was down 11.46 at 2,200.65.
The 30-share DAX in Frankfurt shed 47.37 to 2,799.71 in floor trade and was around 2,802 in later computerised business.
Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average fell more than 500 points before reviving to end down 159.81, 0.78 percent, at 20,341.39.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $369.00 an ounce in the afternoon, compared with $369.05 in the morning and Thursday's London close of $368.45. Silver edged up to $4.84 from $4.82.
